sections.title: Why this module matters
sections.body: Knowing goroutines and channels is table stakes; knowing concurrency patterns is what separates a Go developer who can write code from one who can ship reliable services. Worker pools, pipelines, and error groups are the recurring shapes that appear in real Go backends — job queues, data processing, parallel API fan-out. Interviewers frequently ask candidates to implement these patterns on a whiteboard or in a live coding exercise, and knowing singleflight and semaphore patterns demonstrates awareness of operational hazards like cache stampedes and resource exhaustion.

sections.title: Mental model
sections.body: A **worker pool** is N fixed goroutines all reading from the same buffered job channel — the channel acts as the work queue and back-pressure mechanism. A **pipeline** is a chain of stages connected by channels: stage 1 produces into ch1, stage 2 reads ch1 and produces into ch2, and so on — each stage runs in its own goroutine. A **semaphore** is a buffered channel of capacity N used as a token bucket: acquire by sending a token, release by receiving it, so at most N goroutines run concurrently. `errgroup` wraps WaitGroup with error collection and optional context cancellation, so one failing goroutine cancels all siblings.

sections.title: Must-know concepts
sections.body:
- **Worker pool**: `jobs := make(chan Job, 100)`, launch N workers with `go worker(jobs)`, close jobs channel when done producing, workers exit on channel close.
- **Pipeline pattern**: each stage is a function that takes an input `<-chan T` and returns an output `<-chan U`; compose them to build complex data flows.
- **Semaphore pattern**: `sem := make(chan struct{}, maxConcurrency)` — `sem <- struct{}{}` to acquire, `<-sem` to release; defer release.
- **golang.org/x/sync/errgroup**: `g, ctx := errgroup.WithContext(ctx)`; `g.Go(func() error {...})`; `err := g.Wait()` — first non-nil error cancels the ctx.
- **golang.org/x/sync/singleflight**: `group.Do(key, fn)` — deduplicate concurrent calls with the same key; only one call executes, result shared to all callers.
- **Done-channel shutdown**: `done := make(chan struct{})` closed by the orchestrator signals all workers to stop — prefer context cancellation in modern code.

sections.title: Likely interview hooks
sections.body:
- **"Implement max-50 concurrent workers over 10k tasks"**: create a buffered job channel, launch 50 worker goroutines, feed tasks from main, use WaitGroup to know when all workers are done.
- **singleflight prevents cache stampede**: when 1000 requests miss the cache simultaneously, singleflight ensures only one DB query goes out and all 1000 callers share the result.
- **errgroup.WithContext cancels all goroutines on first error**: any goroutine returning an error causes the group's context to be cancelled, which is why all goroutines must respect ctx.Done().
- **Pipeline goroutine leak**: if a downstream stage exits early without draining the upstream channel, the upstream goroutine blocks forever — use done-channel or context to signal early exit.
- **Buffered vs unbuffered for worker pool jobs channel**: buffered decouples producer from workers and prevents the producer from blocking when all workers are busy.

sections.title: Speaking template
sections.body: "For bounded parallelism I use a worker pool with a buffered job channel — I launch a fixed number of worker goroutines that all read from the same channel, so I get at most N concurrent operations regardless of how many jobs come in. If I need to fan out and collect errors, I reach for errgroup instead of a raw WaitGroup because it handles error propagation and can cancel the whole group's context when one worker fails. For cache stampede protection I add singleflight in front of the DB call — especially on high-traffic endpoints where a cache miss could trigger hundreds of duplicate queries simultaneously. The key thing I always check is that all goroutines have a way to exit: either the input channel is closed, or there's a done channel, or they're respecting context cancellation."
